input.paper_title: Graph-Aware Prompting for Reliable Section Generation
input.paper_venue: ACL Workshop on Natural Language Generation
input.paper_abstract: We present a graph-guided prompting workflow for long-form scientific writing that prioritizes evidence and citation consistency. Our method constructs a document graph that encodes section dependencies and uses strict JSON schemas and evidence-aware prompts to generate and validate individual sections. At generation time, the system (1) builds a section graph and schedules leaf-first writing, (2) retrieves and injects relevant evidence for each section, (3) produces JSON-constrained section outputs, and (4) assembles a LaTeX manuscript with refs.bib. We evaluate the approach by comparing it to a baseline linear prompting pipeline on two topical domains, measuring citation coverage, hallucination rate, and reviewer-style scores. Results show improved citation coverage and reduced unsupported assertions while keeping edits and post-hoc audits straightforward via machine-readable outputs. We intentionally state conservative claims and require explicit source citations for all factual assertions. The paper contributes practical artifacts: a graph-based section scheduler, an evidence-injection protocol per section, and an audit-friendly JSON output format that integrates with standard LaTeX/bib workflows. Our experiments use internal notes and a small curated PDF set where available; metrics focus on citation fidelity and factual consistency rather than broad generalization.

[RID:web:paper:e11122909ad2] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2509.21375v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.21375v1" title="Automated Prompt Generation for Creative and Counterfactual Text-to-image Synthesis"
Text-to-image generation has advanced rapidly with large-scale multimodal training, yet fine-grained controllability remains a critical challenge. Counterfactual controllability, defined as the capacity to deliberately generate images that contradict common-sense patterns, remains a major challenge but plays a crucial role in enabling creativity and exploratory applications. In this work, we address this gap with a focus on counterfactual size (e.g., generating a tiny walrus beside a giant button) and propose an automatic prompt engineering framework that adapts base prompts into revised prompts for counterfactual images. The framework comprises three components: an image evaluator that guides dataset construction by identifying successful image generations, a supervised prompt rewriter that produces revised prompts, and a DPO-trained ranker that selects the optimal revised prompt. We construct the first counterfactual size text-image dataset and enhance the image evaluator by extending Grounded SAM with refinements, achieving a 114 percent improvement over its backbone. Experiments demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines and ChatGPT-4o, establishing a foundation for future research on counterfactual controllability.

Previously published templates were based on small samples of luminous galaxies, not necessarily representative of normal star-forming galaxies. We construct new dust templates, including instrument-specific relations and software tools that facilitate the estimation of the TIR luminosity and SFR based on one or several fluxes up to z=4. For the first time the templates include a dependence on both TIR luminosity and the sSFR, thereby increasing their reliability and utility. We also provide formulae for calculating TIR luminosities and SFR from JWST F2100W observations at 0<z<2. [RID:web:paper:ddf6cdc71f1d] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2212.11685v2" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2212.11685v2" title="Text Generation with Diffusion Language Models: A Pre-training Approach with Continuous Paragraph Denoise"
In this paper, we introduce a novel dIffusion language modEl pre-training framework for text generation, which we call GENIE. GENIE is a large-scale pretrained diffusion language model that consists of an encoder and a diffusion-based decoder, which can generate text by gradually transforming a random noise sequence into a coherent text sequence. To pre-train GENIE on a large-scale language corpus, we design a new continuous paragraph denoise objective, which encourages the diffusion-decoder to reconstruct a clean text paragraph from a corrupted version, while preserving the semantic and syntactic coherence. We evaluate GENIE on four downstream text generation benchmarks, namely XSum, CNN/DailyMail, Gigaword, and CommonGen. Our experimental results show that GENIE achieves comparable performance with the state-of-the-art autoregressive models on these benchmarks, and generates more diverse text samples. The code and models of GENIE are available at https://github.com/microsoft/ProphetNet/tree/master/GENIE.

[RID:web:paper:d8a0374acd13] kind=web source="arXiv" loc="arXiv" score=1.00 cite_key="2401.06105v1" url="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.06105v1" title="PALP: Prompt Aligned Personalization of Text-to-Image Models"
Content creators often aim to create personalized images using personal subjects that go beyond the capabilities of conventional text-to-image models. Additionally, they may want the resulting image to encompass a specific location, style, ambiance, and more. Existing personalization methods may compromise personalization ability or the alignment to complex textual prompts. This trade-off can impede the fulfillment of user prompts and subject fidelity. We propose a new approach focusing on personalization methods for a \emph{single} prompt to address this issue. We term our approach prompt-aligned personalization. While this may seem restrictive, our method excels in improving text alignment, enabling the creation of images with complex and intricate prompts, which may pose a challenge for current techniques. In particular, our method keeps the personalized model aligned with a target prompt using an additional score distillation sampling term. We demonstrate the versatility of our method in multi- and single-shot settings and further show that it can compose multiple subjects or use inspiration from reference images, such as artworks. We compare our approach quantitatively and qualitatively with existing baselines and state-of-the-art techniques.
input.section_draft:
We design prompt templates that explicitly prioritize the inclusion and anchoring of retrieved evidence and that constrain the model to emit machine-parseable JSON for each section. The templates are organized into three complementary families—Evidence-Anchor Prompts, JSON-Constraint Prompts, and Repair/Validation Prompts—and are intended to be used in a short iterative loop that alternates generation and automated checks. Below we describe the template components, the required JSON structure for a section, the evidence-anchoring conventions, and the iterative generation/validation procedure.

Prompt components
- Context block (fixed): a concise description of the target section (section role, expected scope, and dependency edges from the section graph). This block is strictly descriptive and contains no model-produced claims.
- Evidence block (variable): a ranked list of retrieved items provided as numbered evidence entries. Each entry includes a short citation key, a one-line provenance note, and a quoted excerpt or summary of the supporting text. The prompt instructs the model that every factual assertion in the section must cite one or more of these numbered evidence entries by index.
- Instruction block (fixed): explicit, stepwise instructions that require (a) citation-first composition (list the evidence indices that will support each paragraph before the paragraph text), (b) emission of the prescribed JSON fields only, and (c) conservative language for any claim not covered by the supplied evidence.
- Output block (fixed): an exact machine-readable JSON schema description (see below) and an explicit statement that any output not matching the schema will be rejected and must be regenerated.

JSON schema for a section (illustrative)
- section_id: string (required) — canonical node identifier from the section graph.
- title: string (required) — short section heading text.
- citations: list of objects (required) — each object: {evidence_idx: integer, source_label: string, bib_entry_id: string_or_null}.
- paragraphs: list of objects (required) — each object: {lead_evidence: [integer], text: string, inline_evidence_anchors: [{evidence_idx: integer, char_span: [start,end]}]}.
- claims: list of objects (optional but recommended) — each object: {claim_text: string, supporting_evidence: [integer], confidence: string_enum(low,medium,high)}.
- validation_notes: object (required) — {schema_valid: boolean, missing_evidence: [paragraph_index], unsupported_assertions_found: boolean, remediation_suggestion: string}.
Constraints and validation rules are stated in the prompt (for example: ``paragraphs must be non-empty; each paragraph must list at least one lead_evidence; inline_evidence_anchors must reference evidence indices present in citations''). Templates include exact field names and types to avoid model-driven renaming.

Evidence-anchoring conventions
- Numbered evidence indices: evidence items are addressed by short integer indices (1,2,3,...) to reduce token length and enforce unambiguous anchors.
- Citation-first paragraph header: before each paragraph text, the model must output the list of lead_evidence indices that substantiate the forthcoming paragraph. This ordering makes it straightforward to check whether any paragraph lacks evidence coverage.
- Inline anchors with spans: models are asked to provide character-span anchors that localize which substring of the paragraph is supported by which evidence index. These spans are used by validators (automated or human) to rapidly assess alignment between claim text and evidence.
- Bib integration: when retrieved items map to bibliographic records, prompts require the model to populate bib_entry_id where available; otherwise bib_entry_id may be null but must be indicated.

Iterative generation and validation loop
1) Retrieval and prompt assembly: retrieve ranked evidence for the target section and assemble the Context + Evidence + Instruction + Output blocks into a single prompt.
2) Generation: request a single JSON-constrained response from the model using the Evidence-Anchor Prompt + JSON-Constraint Prompt. The model must output only the JSON described above.
3) Automated schema validation: run a strict JSON schema validator. If the response fails validation, apply the Repair/Validation Prompt and retry generation; keep a capped number of automated retries.
4) Citation-coverage checks: verify that each paragraph lists at least one lead_evidence and that all inline_evidence_anchors reference defined evidence indices. Flag paragraphs with missing coverage as candidates for evidence augmentation.
5) Unsupported-claim detection (conservative): run a lightweight surface check for sentences that (a) contain factual predicates and (b) lack any inline_evidence_anchors. If detected, mark as unsupported assertions and include details in validation_notes.
6) Repair strategies: (a) regenerate the paragraph with higher emphasis on evidence anchors; (b) augment the evidence set (retrieve additional items) and re-prompt; or (c) escalate to a human reviewer when automated repair fails or when the validation_notes indicate high-risk unsupported assertions.
7) Commit or stage: accept the JSON output for assembly only if schema_valid is true and unsupported_assertions_found is false or explicitly acknowledged and remedied; otherwise stage the section for human review.

Template examples (format guidance)
- Evidence-Anchor Prompt excerpt (natural language guidance, included in prompt): ``For each paragraph, first list the evidence indices that will support it, e.g. [2,5]. Then write the paragraph. For each factual phrase, add an inline_evidence_anchors entry that gives the evidence_idx and character-span for the supported substring.''
- JSON-Constraint Prompt excerpt: ``Emit only valid JSON matching the following schema. Do not include commentary outside the JSON. If you cannot support a claim with the provided evidence, state that you cannot make the claim in the relevant paragraph's text.''

Design motivations and conservative stance
- The templates are intentionally prescriptive: requiring citation-first paragraphs and explicit evidence spans trades higher prompt strictness and human-reviewable structure for reductions in unsupported assertions during downstream assembly. Statements about empirical effectiveness are not made here; empirical evaluation is reported in the Experiments and Results sections. (General background knowledge: structured, evidence-anchored outputs are commonly used to improve auditability in retrieval-augmented generation; we do not cite external sources here because no retrieved excerpts were provided.)

Practical notes and limitations
- Schema brittleness: strict JSON constraints reduce ambiguity but increase the need for repair loops when models deviate from schema (handled by the Repair/Validation Prompt and capped retries).
- Retrieval dependence: the approach assumes a retrieval set that contains sufficiently relevant items; when retrieval fails to return supporting evidence, the templates default to conservative language and flag unsupported assertions for human review.
- Human-in-the-loop thresholds: our workflow treats any paragraph with no lead_evidence as requiring human adjudication; these thresholds are configurable but must be stated explicitly in system configuration.

In sum, the evidence-aware prompt templates combine explicit evidence presentation, citation-first paragraph structure, and a strict JSON output contract to make section generation both machine-parseable and audit-friendly. The iterative generation/validation loop operationalizes conservative failure handling: automated repair is attempted first, and unresolved unsupported assertions are routed for human review.
